about: Lesson X2 (x02-fossil-transition), side-topic shelf, Analyst, D2, wave W6, builder learn-w6-x, 2026-11-07. What gas networks, LNG, gas and coal plants, coal mines, oil, carbon capture and carbon removal do in the U.S. system today, with dated EIA, IEA, LBNL and IPCC sources; a year of coal retirement plans against retirements; a gas network's cost over fewer customers and a plant's unrecovered cost (both illustrative, set for teaching); carbon-removal methods compared by permanence, readiness, cost range, potential and measurement (IPCC AR6 WGIII, 2022). Neutral: no forecast, no verdict. Text with {tokens} is filled from these numbers by the lesson's script.

predictRetire.q: How much of the planned 8.5 GW retired in 2025

assume.label: No pipe retired
assume.line: The whole network stays, so the customers who remain share its whole assumed cost.

assume.label: Pipes to leavers retired
assume.line: Half of the leavers' share of the cost is avoided by retiring the pipes that served them.

gasNet.set: teaching: one network cost of $500 per customer a year, split equally among the customers who stay, and the share of a leaver's cost that retiring pipes avoids (0 or 50%); not a real utility's numbers

book.set: teaching: the building cost recovered evenly (straight line) over a 40-year book life; real plants follow their regulators' and owners' schedules

predictCcs.q: A coal plant that captures 90% of its CO₂: carbon removal

options.label: Yes: the CO₂ is stored underground
No: it cuts its emissions but takes none out of the air

feedback.yes: No: storing a plant's own CO₂ cuts its emissions; removal takes CO₂ that is already in the air (IPCC).
feedback.no: Yes: IPCC says capture applied to fossil fuel use is not removal, since it takes no CO₂ out of the air.
feedback.ten: No: storage time matters for removal, but a coal plant's capture takes no CO₂ out of the air at all (IPCC).

cdr.title: Six ways to remove carbon, compared
cdr.note: Cost: U.S. dollars per tonne of CO₂, IPCC's author-judgement ranges from studies in different dollar years, not adjusted to one year. A low end below zero is an estimated net saving.
cdr.note2: Potential: billions of tonnes of CO₂ a year that the literature finds possible, not today's scale.
cdr.trlScale: Readiness: 1 = basic principles described, 9 = proven in operation.
cdr.beccsWhy: Why BECCS can count as removal: plants take CO₂ from the air as they grow; storing that carbon after the biomass is used can give net removal, once other emissions and land-carbon losses are counted.

rows.name: Direct air capture with storage (DACCS)
rows.measure: Count the CO₂ stored, less emissions from the energy and water it uses.

rows.name: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS)
rows.measure: Count the CO₂ stored, less emissions and land carbon lost growing the biomass.

rows.name: Enhanced weathering (crushed rock on fields)
rows.measure: How fast the rock takes up CO₂ in real soils is still poorly quantified.

rows.name: Biochar (charred plant matter in soil)
rows.store: Soils: decades to centuries (IPCC's timescale for carbon stored in soils)
rows.measure: Count the carbon in the char, less emissions from making it.

rows.name: Afforestation and reforestation
rows.store: Trees and soils: decades to centuries
rows.measure: Carbon in growing trees; wildfire, disease or pests can reverse it.

rows.name: Soil carbon in croplands and grasslands
rows.measure: IPCC: the net addition per hectare is very small and hard to monitor.

sorts.label: By how long it stores
sorts.note: Longest storage first: geological formations and minerals, then trees and soils. Ties keep the table's order.

sorts.label: By readiness
sorts.note: Most ready first, by the middle of IPCC's readiness range (1 basic principles to 9 proven in operation). Ties keep the table's order.

sorts.label: By cost range, low end
sorts.note: Lowest end of IPCC's cost range first; a low end says nothing of a project's real cost.

steelman.title: Is gas a bridge or a lock-in? The strongest case on each side

sides.title: A bridge
points: Burning gas for power emitted {co2gas} lb of CO₂ per kWh of electricity generated in 2023 against coal's {co2coal} (EIA, utility-scale, burning only).
Gas plants already make {gasShare} of U.S. utility-scale electricity, on networks that exist today.

sides.title: A lock-in
points: Gas networks last decades: EIA reported in March 2024 that about half of the long-distance gas pipeline network went in during the 1950s and 1960s.
Leaks before burning narrow the gap: one study put U.S. oil and gas methane at {methane} of gas produced in 2015 (Alvarez et al. 2018, abstract).

sides.title: What would tell them apart
points: How many hours new gas plants run in later decades, and measured leak rates ([[lesson:f11-air-climate-people|F11]] counts leaks as CO₂e).

steelman.note: Both cases from dated sources; the lesson takes no side.
